questions.stem: A 41 year old man grazed his left shin on a garden fence 2 days ago. He now has excruciating pain in the lower leg and needs morphine, yet there is only faint pink erythema with mild swelling. His temperature is 38.9°C, pulse rate 124 bpm, BP 94/58 mmHg and respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Severe pain far beyond the faint skin signs, after a minor injury, with sepsis, is necrotising fasciitis.

steps.x: Pain out of proportion to the skin, systemic illness and a minor wound.

elim: Pain matches the visible redness and the patient is rarely this shocked.
Follows fractures or crush injury, not a graze with fever and sepsis.
Causes calf swelling without fever, tachycardia and hypotension.
A superficial infection with a raised, sharply demarcated edge, pain proportionate.

steps.x: E: Necrotising fasciitis. Pain out of proportion plus systemic illness = necrotising fasciitis until proven otherwise.

questions.stem: A 29 year old man had a crush injury to his thigh in a motorbike crash 2 days ago, with a deep contaminated wound. The thigh is now swollen and bronze-brown with foul-smelling discharge. Pressing the skin produces a crackling sensation. His temperature is 39.2°C, pulse rate 130 bpm and BP 86/50 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely causative organism?
questions.e: A deep contaminated crush wound with crepitus is gas gangrene, caused by Clostridium perfringens.

steps.x: Crepitus means gas in the tissues after a deep dirty wound.

elim: Causes green-pus wound infections, not gas-forming myonecrosis.
Causes abscesses and cellulitis; gas in tissue is not its feature.
A low-virulence coloniser of lines and prostheses.
Causes type 2 necrotising fasciitis but does not typically produce gas.

steps.x: A: Clostridium perfringens. Crepitus after a deep contaminated wound = gas gangrene = Clostridium perfringens.

questions.stem: A 61 year old man with poorly controlled type 2 diabetes has a 36 hour history of severe pain and swelling of his scrotum and perineum. The scrotal skin is dusky purple with a small black area and the perineum is exquisitely tender. His temperature is 38.6°C, pulse rate 118 bpm and BP 100/62 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Necrotising fasciitis of the scrotum and perineum in a diabetic is Fournier's gangrene.

steps.x: Diabetic man, necrotic scrotal skin, systemic illness.

elim: Causes a tender testis with urinary symptoms, not skin necrosis and sepsis.
Causes a groin lump, not black scrotal skin with fever.
A localised fluctuant swelling; no spreading skin necrosis.
Sudden testicular pain in young men, no fever or skin necrosis.

steps.x: B: Fournier's gangrene. Necrotising fasciitis of the scrotum or vulva = Fournier's gangrene; the perineum is the commonest site.

questions.stem: A 55 year old woman is on the surgical ward with suspected infection of her right thigh after a fall onto gravel. Over 12 hours a central area of the red, swollen thigh has turned black and is now numb, surrounded by haemorrhagic bullae. Her pulse rate is 122 bpm and BP 92/56 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely explanation for the black area of skin?
questions.e: A black, numb patch of skin in a spreading soft tissue infection indicates tissue necrosis.

steps.x: A black, numb area appearing within hours inside an infected area.

elim: Bruising does not appear 12 hours into an infection with bullae and sepsis.
A small painless scab at a bite site, not a spreading black patch.
Brown staining of chronic venous disease, develops over months.
A slowly changing pigmented lesion, not an acute area in an infected limb.

steps.x: E: Tissue necrosis. A black patch of skin in a soft tissue infection = necrosis from small vessel thrombosis.

questions.stem: A 33 year old woman who injects heroin into her groin has a 1 day history of rapidly spreading redness and severe pain around the injection site. The redness has crept 6 cm past the pen line drawn 4 hours ago. Her temperature is 39.0°C, pulse rate 128 bpm, BP 90/54 mmHg and she is confused.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: IV drug use is a risk factor; spread over hours with severe pain and septic shock is necrotising fasciitis.

clues: crept 6 cm past the pen line
steps.x: A risk factor (IV drug use), very rapid spread and a septic, confused patient.

elim: A pulsatile groin mass, not rapidly spreading erythema with sepsis.
A localised fluctuant collection that does not spread centimetres per hour.
Causes fever and murmurs, not a spreading painful skin infection.
A tender cord along a vein with little systemic upset.

steps.x: D: Necrotising fasciitis. Rapid spread past the marked edge plus sepsis = necrotising fasciitis.

questions.stem: A 48 year old man has a red, swollen left forearm 1 day after a cat scratch. He is in severe pain, the erythema has no clear edge, and touching the skin well beyond the red area makes him cry out. His temperature is 38.7°C and pulse rate 116 bpm.
questions.q: Which feature most strongly suggests necrotising fasciitis rather than cellulitis?
o: A history of an animal scratch
questions.e: Pain and tenderness extending beyond the visible changes shows the deep fascia is involved before the skin.

steps.x: Poorly demarcated erythema and tenderness past the skin changes.

elim: Animal scratches commonly cause simple cellulitis.
Fever is common in cellulitis too.
Swelling occurs in both conditions.
Warm skin is typical of cellulitis.

steps.x: D: Tenderness beyond the visible erythema. Pain disproportionate to and beyond the skin findings separates necrotising fasciitis from cellulitis.

questions.stem: A 58 year old man with necrotising fasciitis of the abdominal wall refused surgery 12 hours ago. He is now drowsy and mottled. His pulse rate is 140 bpm, BP 70/38 mmHg despite 3 litres of IV fluid, and he has passed 20 mL of urine in 4 hours.
questions.q: Which is the most likely complication?
questions.e: Untreated necrotising fasciitis progresses rapidly to septic shock and organ failure (here kidneys and brain).

clues: BP 70/38 mmHg despite 3 litres of IV fluid
steps.x: Delayed debridement, fluid-resistant hypotension and oliguria.

elim: Would cause urticaria and wheeze after a dose, not a steady decline with infection.
No chest trauma or features such as raised JVP and muffled heart sounds.
There is no source of blood loss; fluids have not helped.
Causes sudden breathlessness and hypoxia, not oliguria with mottling from infection.

steps.x: E: Septic shock with multi-organ failure. Delay in debridement leads to septic shock, multi-organ failure, amputation or death.

questions.stem: A 66 year old woman with type 2 diabetes develops severe vulval and perineal pain with spreading dusky erythema and fever. Her medications are metformin, empagliflozin, ramipril and atorvastatin.
questions.q: Which of her medications most increased her risk of this infection?
questions.e: SGLT-2 inhibitors such as empagliflozin cause glycosuria and are linked to Fournier's gangrene.

steps.x: Genital necrotising fasciitis in a diabetic on an SGLT-2 inhibitor.

elim: Statins cause myopathy, not genital infections.
Causes GI upset and lactic acidosis, not genital soft tissue infection.
Causes cough, hyperkalaemia and angioedema.
A DPP-4 inhibitor not taken by her and not linked to genital infection.

steps.x: B: Empagliflozin. SGLT-2 inhibitors (the -gliflozins) are linked to Fournier's gangrene.

questions.stem: A 72 year old man had an open inguinal hernia repair 3 days ago. He now has severe wound pain, a tense swollen groin with greyish discharge, and spreading erythema onto the abdominal wall. His temperature is 38.8°C, pulse rate 120 bpm and BP 96/60 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Severe pain, spreading erythema, dishwater discharge and sepsis after surgery indicates necrotising fasciitis.

clues: spreading erythema onto the abdominal wall
steps.x: Recent surgery, rapid spread and systemic illness.

elim: A collection of blood without fever, spreading erythema and sepsis.
A tender irreducible lump with bowel obstruction, not spreading infection.
A painless fluid collection without systemic upset.
Localised redness at the wound without severe pain or shock.

steps.x: C: Necrotising fasciitis. Necrotising fasciitis often follows minor injury or surgery; think of it when a wound looks worse by the hour.

questions.stem: A 50 year old woman was admitted 24 hours ago with what was thought to be cellulitis of the right leg. Despite IV flucloxacillin, the skin now has tense violaceous bullae, patches of grey-black discolouration and crepitus on palpation. Her pulse rate is 126 bpm.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Later features of necrotising fasciitis are bullae, gangrenous skin and crepitus.

steps.x: Bullae, gangrene-like skin and gas developing on a 'cellulitis'.

elim: Tense itchy blisters in the elderly without infection or crepitus.
Cellulitis does not produce crepitus or gangrenous skin.
Target lesions after infection or drugs, no necrosis or gas.
Mucosal involvement and skin detachment after a drug, no crepitus.

steps.x: D: Necrotising fasciitis. Cellulitis that progresses to bullae, necrosis and crepitus is necrotising fasciitis.

questions.stem: A 44 year old woman taking azathioprine and prednisolone after a liver transplant has a 1 day history of severe pain in her left calf. Examination shows only mild swelling and slight redness. Her temperature is 38.4°C, pulse rate 118 bpm and lactate 4.6 mmol/L. Doppler ultrasound of the leg veins is normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: In immunosuppressed patients skin signs lag behind the deep infection; severe pain with sepsis is necrotising fasciitis.

clues: only mild swelling and slight redness
steps.x: Immunosuppression, minimal skin signs, severe pain and sepsis.

elim: Causes calf pain and swelling but not fever and raised lactate.
Pain would match the redness; this degree of sepsis is unusual.
The Doppler is normal.
No fever, sepsis or raised lactate.

steps.x: E: Necrotising fasciitis. Skin is spared early, so mild skin signs never exclude necrotising fasciitis.

questions.stem: A 69 year old man with type 2 diabetes and obesity is admitted with a temperature of 38.7°C, pulse rate 122 bpm and severe pain far beyond a patch of mild erythema. The surgical registrar suspects necrotising fasciitis and wants to examine the site most commonly affected overall.
questions.q: Which is the most likely affected site?
questions.e: The perineum is the most commonly affected site overall, as in Fournier's gangrene.

steps.x: A diabetic man, the group at highest risk of Fournier's gangrene.

elim: Can follow surgery but is less common than the perineum.
A rare site.
Can follow injury but is less common.
Less common than the perineum.

steps.x: D: Perineum. Perineum is the most commonly affected site overall.

questions.stem: A 38 year old man has severe pain in his right forearm 2 days after a splinter injury, with mild erythema and swelling. His temperature is 39.1°C, pulse rate 128 bpm and BP 88/52 mmHg. The surgical registrar suspects necrotising fasciitis.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate way to confirm the diagnosis?
questions.e: Necrotising fasciitis is a clinical diagnosis confirmed at surgery; imaging must not delay theatre.

steps.x: A shocked patient with clinical features of necrotising fasciitis.

elim: Imaging may show gas but must never delay surgery in a shocked patient.
Takes time; imaging must never delay surgery.
Results take days and do not change immediate management.
Identifies organisms later but cannot confirm necrotising fasciitis.

steps.x: A: Clinical assessment and surgical exploration. Clinical diagnosis; imaging must never delay surgery.

questions.stem: A 52 year old woman has a painful, swollen left thigh after an insect bite, with mild erythema. She is haemodynamically stable. A bedside ultrasound is performed to look for deeper infection.
questions.q: Which is the most likely ultrasound finding if she has necrotising fasciitis?
o: A discrete hypoechoic collection with a wall
Fluid and air along the deep fascia
questions.e: Fluid and air between fascial layers on ultrasound indicates deeper soft tissue infection.

steps.x: Ultrasound is used to look beneath the skin for deep infection.

elim: Describes an abscess.
Typical of cellulitis and oedema.
Describes a deep vein thrombosis.
Necrotising fasciitis changes the fascial planes.

steps.x: C: Fluid and air along the deep fascia. Fluid and air tracking along the fascia = deep necrotising infection.

questions.stem: A 46 year old man with type 2 diabetes has necrotising fasciitis of the perineum. He is breathing rapidly. A venous blood gas and bloods are taken.
questions.q: Which is the most likely set of blood results?
o: Low CRP and WCC with respiratory acidosis
Normal CRP and WCC with metabolic alkalosis
Raised CRP and WCC with metabolic acidosis
Raised CRP and WCC with metabolic alkalosis
questions.e: Blood tests show raised CRP and WCC with a metabolic (lactic) acidosis.

steps.x: Severe infection plus Kussmaul-type breathing from acidosis.

elim: Severe sepsis raises inflammatory markers; rapid breathing gives a low CO2.
Overwhelming infection raises markers and causes acidosis.
Sepsis causes lactic acidosis, not alkalosis.
Eosinophilia suggests allergy or parasites.

steps.x: C: Raised CRP and WCC with metabolic acidosis. Bloods: raised CRP and WCC, metabolic acidosis.

questions.stem: A 63 year old woman has suspected necrotising fasciitis of the left leg. IV meropenem and clindamycin have been started. The surgeons are ready to take her to theatre now. Her BP is 92/54 mmHg after fluids. A junior doctor asks whether an MRI of the leg should be arranged first.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate response?
o: Arrange CT of the leg before theatre
Arrange MRI of the leg before theatre
questions.e: CT or MRI may show gas within tissues, but imaging must never delay surgical debridement.

clues: ready to take her to theatre now
steps.x: The team is ready and the patient is unstable.

elim: Imaging must never delay surgery.
MRI can show gas but must never delay surgery.
Delays surgery and gas may be absent.
Cultures guide later antibiotics and never delay debridement.

steps.x: C: Go to theatre without imaging. Imaging must never delay surgery in necrotising fasciitis.

questions.stem: A 59 year old man has a 2 day history of severe pain in his right buttock after an intramuscular injection. Crepitus is felt on palpation. A plain X-ray of the pelvis is taken.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on the X-ray?
questions.e: Crepitus reflects gas in the tissues, which imaging may show.

steps.x: Crepitus means gas in the soft tissues.

elim: Suggests osteomyelitis, develops over weeks.
Crepitus implies gas, which X-ray can show.
A feature of chronic bone infection or tumour.
Seen in chronic conditions such as dermatomyositis.

steps.x: B: Gas in the soft tissues. Imaging may show soft tissue gas, but it must never delay surgery.

questions.stem: A 35 year old man has a 1 day history of a red, warm right calf after a football graze. His temperature is 38.1°C. The emergency doctor is deciding between cellulitis and necrotising fasciitis and has not yet requested any imaging.
questions.q: Which additional finding would most strongly suggest necrotising fasciitis?
o: A well-demarcated edge to the erythema
Pain disproportionate to the skin findings
Tenderness limited to the red area
questions.e: The diagnosis is clinical: pain out of proportion plus systemic illness separates necrotising fasciitis from cellulitis.

clues: deciding between cellulitis and necrotising fasciitis
has not yet requested any imaging
steps.x: The choice is clinical, between two skin infections.

elim: A sharp edge favours erysipelas or cellulitis.
Necrotising fasciitis causes systemic illness.
Non-specific; occurs in cellulitis and heart failure.
Proportionate tenderness suits cellulitis.

steps.x: C: Pain disproportionate to the skin findings. Pain disproportionate to exam findings is the hallmark of necrotising fasciitis.

questions.stem: A 70 year old man has Fournier's gangrene of the scrotum. He has received a fluid bolus and IV antibiotics in the emergency department. His BP is now 104/66 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate definitive management?
o: Urinary catheter and review in 24 hours
questions.e: Emergency surgical debridement of all necrotic tissue is definitive management.

steps.x: Fournier's gangrene is necrotising fasciitis.

elim: Not definitive and must not delay surgery.
Antibiotics cannot penetrate necrotic tissue; surgery is needed.
The testes are usually spared; the necrotic fascia and skin must be removed.
Delay is fatal.

steps.x: A: Emergency surgical debridement. Definitive management of necrotising fasciitis is emergency surgical debridement.

questions.stem: A 45 year old woman has suspected necrotising fasciitis of the left thigh. She has no drug allergies. The surgeons are on their way and the emergency doctor is choosing empirical IV antibiotics.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate empirical antibiotic regimen?
questions.e: Empirical cover is IV broad-spectrum: meropenem or piperacillin-tazobactam, plus clindamycin.

steps.x: A life-threatening, possibly polymicrobial infection.

elim: Too narrow for a polymicrobial or toxin-producing infection.
Treats cellulitis, not a life-threatening necrotising infection.
Oral therapy is inadequate in a septic patient.
Lacks Gram-negative and anaerobic cover and toxin suppression.

steps.x: C: Meropenem plus clindamycin. Piperacillin-tazobactam or meropenem, plus clindamycin.

questions.stem: A 64 year old man with suspected necrotising fasciitis of the right leg arrives in the emergency department. His pulse rate is 132 bpm, BP 82/48 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 92% breathing air. The surgical team will be 20 minutes.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
o: Mark the erythema and review in 4 hours
questions.e: While surgery is arranged, the Sepsis Six (oxygen, cultures, IV antibiotics, fluids, lactate, urine output) is started.

clues: The surgical team will be 20 minutes
steps.x: Septic shock with a short wait for theatre.

elim: Imaging must never delay management.
He is shocked; delay is dangerous.
He has septic shock.
No suggestion of thrombosis.

steps.x: E: Start the Sepsis Six. Supportive care with the Sepsis Six runs alongside urgent surgery.

questions.stem: A 57 year old woman has had debridement of necrotising fasciitis of the abdominal wall. After surgery her BP is 78/40 mmHg despite 4 litres of crystalloid, and her lactate is 6.2 mmol/L.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next step?
o: Discharge to the ward with oral antibiotics
Refer to critical care for vasopressors
Repeat CT abdomen before any treatment
Stop antibiotics now the tissue is removed
questions.e: Fluid-refractory septic shock needs critical care support with vasopressors.

steps.x: Hypotension and raised lactate despite fluids.

elim: She is in refractory septic shock.
Worsens hypotension.
Imaging must not delay resuscitation.
Antibiotics continue after debridement.

steps.x: C: Refer to critical care for vasopressors. Supportive care includes critical care support as needed.

questions.stem: A 40 year old man with necrotising fasciitis due to Streptococcus pyogenes is given IV piperacillin-tazobactam. The microbiologist recommends adding a second antibiotic to reduce bacterial toxin production.
questions.q: Which antibiotic is most appropriate to add?
questions.e: Clindamycin is added to piperacillin-tazobactam or meropenem; it inhibits protein synthesis and so toxin production.

steps.x: A toxin-producing streptococcus already on a beta-lactam.

elim: Not used for toxin suppression in necrotising infection.
A bacteriostatic oral agent not used here.
Gram-negative cover only; no effect on toxin production.
Anaerobic cover but no toxin suppression in streptococcal infection.

steps.x: B: Clindamycin. Piperacillin-tazobactam plus clindamycin: clindamycin switches off toxins.

questions.stem: A 68 year old man with diabetes had debridement of necrotising fasciitis of the right foot and leg 2 days ago. Despite two further debridements, the infection keeps spreading up the leg and he remains in septic shock.
questions.q: Which is the most likely next surgical step?
questions.e: When repeated debridement fails to control spread, amputation may be needed to save life.

steps.x: Ongoing spread despite repeated debridement.

elim: He is in septic shock.
Does not control spreading infection.
Grafting comes only after infection is controlled.
Cannot control a deep spreading infection.

steps.x: A: Amputation of the limb. Complications include amputation; source control saves the patient.

questions.stem: A 31 year old man has suspected necrotising fasciitis of the left arm after a dog bite. His BP is 90/56 mmHg. IV antibiotics and fluids have been given. The radiographer can do an MRI in 3 hours.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
questions.e: Suspected necrotising fasciitis in a shocked patient needs immediate surgical debridement.

steps.x: Shock and a 3-hour wait for imaging.

elim: Imaging must never delay surgery.
Inadequate for a necrotising infection.
He is shocked; delay worsens outcome.
Not first-line and delays surgery.

steps.x: D: Proceed to emergency surgical debridement. Clinical suspicion is enough: debride now.

questions.stem: A 24 year old previously healthy woman cut her knee while hiking. Three days later she has necrotising fasciitis of the leg. Blood cultures grow Gram-positive cocci in chains that are beta-haemolytic on blood agar.
questions.q: Which is the most likely causative organism?
questions.e: Monomicrobial (type 2) necrotising fasciitis is most commonly caused by Group A Streptococcus.

steps.x: Beta-haemolytic cocci in chains in a healthy young person.

elim: A Gram-positive rod causing gas gangrene.
A Gram-negative rod, part of polymicrobial type 1 infection.
Gram-positive cocci in clusters.
Alpha-haemolytic diplococci causing pneumonia.

steps.x: E: Streptococcus pyogenes. Type 2 = Group A Streptococcus (S. pyogenes); type 1 = polymicrobial.

questions.stem: A 67 year old man with diabetes and peripheral vascular disease has necrotising fasciitis of the perineum. Tissue samples grow Escherichia coli, Bacteroides fragilis and an Enterococcus species.
questions.q: Which is the most accurate classification of his infection?
questions.e: Mixed aerobic and anaerobic organisms define type 1 (polymicrobial) necrotising fasciitis.

clues: Escherichia coli, Bacteroides fragilis and an Enterococcus
steps.x: Several different organisms grown together.

elim: A superficial streptococcal infection.
Caused by Clostridium perfringens.
A toxin syndrome, not a classification of necrotising fasciitis.
Usually caused by Group A Streptococcus alone.

steps.x: D: Type 1 polymicrobial necrotising fasciitis. Polymicrobial = type 1; Group A Streptococcus = type 2.

questions.stem: A 37 year old man has severe pain in his thigh with only mild overlying erythema. At surgery the subcutaneous tissue and deep fascia are grey, necrotic and easily separated by a finger, while the overlying skin looks almost normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of spread?
o: Bacterial enzymes and toxins destroying tissue along fascial planes
Immune complex deposition in vessel walls
Spread through the bloodstream to muscle
questions.e: Exotoxins, hyaluronidase and streptokinase destroy fascia and subcutaneous tissue along fascial planes, sparing skin initially.

steps.x: Deep tissue destroyed while the skin is spared.

elim: The skin is relatively spared; spread is along the fascia.
Describes vasculitis.
Describes erysipelas.
Muscle is relatively spared initially.

steps.x: A: Bacterial enzymes and toxins destroying tissue along fascial planes. Enzymes spread along fascial planes; skin lags behind, so signs underestimate severity.

questions.stem: A 34 year old man has gas gangrene of the calf after a deep farm injury. Tissue samples grow Gram-positive rods. At surgery the muscle is pale, does not contract and does not bleed when cut.
questions.q: Which bacterial product is most responsible for the muscle damage?
questions.e: Clostridium perfringens alpha-toxin causes myonecrosis and gas production.

steps.x: Clostridium (Gram-positive rod) with dead muscle.

elim: Found in Gram-negative bacteria.
Produced by Streptococcus pyogenes in scarlet fever.
A streptococcal enzyme, not clostridial.
Clostridium tetani toxin causing spasms, not myonecrosis.

steps.x: A: Alpha-toxin. C. perfringens alpha-toxin: myonecrosis plus gas = crepitus.

questions.stem: A 62 year old woman with necrotising fasciitis of the arm has a new black area on her forearm. Histology after debridement shows thrombi blocking small dermal blood vessels.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of the black skin?
o: Bleeding into the skin from low platelets
Ischaemic necrosis from small vessel thrombosis
questions.e: Thrombosis of small vessels supplying the skin causes ischaemia and necrosis, so it turns black.

clues: thrombi blocking small dermal blood vessels
steps.x: Clotted small vessels on histology.

elim: Causes purpura, not black necrotic skin.
Bacteria do not pigment the skin black.
Melanocytes are not the target.
Causes swelling and purple skin, not necrosis with arterial thrombi.

steps.x: D: Ischaemic necrosis from small vessel thrombosis. Black skin = small vessel thrombosis, ischaemia and necrosis.

questions.stem: A 57 year old man with type 2 diabetes started dapagliflozin 3 months ago. He now has Fournier's gangrene. A student asks why this medication increases the risk.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism?
o: Glycosuria promoting bacterial growth in the genital region
Reduced skin blood flow from vasoconstriction
questions.e: SGLT-2 inhibitors block glucose reabsorption, and the resulting glycosuria promotes local bacterial growth.

steps.x: An SGLT-2 inhibitor and a genital infection.

elim: SGLT-2 inhibitors rarely cause hypoglycaemia.
Linked to metformin, not genital infection.
Not a mechanism of SGLT-2 inhibitors.
SGLT-2 inhibitors are not immunosuppressants.

steps.x: A: Glycosuria promoting bacterial growth in the genital region. SGLT-2 inhibitor -> glycosuria -> genital bacterial growth -> Fournier's gangrene.

questions.stem: A 49 year old woman had a small leg wound in the morning. By evening she has necrotising fasciitis and by the next morning she is in septic shock. A student asks why it progresses so quickly.
questions.q: Which is the most likely explanation?
o: Rapid fascial spread with systemic absorption of bacterial toxins
Slow lymphatic spread to the lungs
questions.e: Rapid spread along fascial planes plus absorption of bacterial toxins causes swift progression to shock if debridement is delayed.

clues: by the next morning she is in septic shock
steps.x: Hours from wound to shock.

elim: Septic shock is not an IgE-mediated reaction.
There is no significant haemorrhage.
Cannot explain shock this fast.
Spread is rapid and along fascial planes.

steps.x: D: Rapid fascial spread with systemic absorption of bacterial toxins. Fast fascial spread plus toxins = shock unless debrided early.
